subject: history
topicDisplay: Crime Punishment C1000 Present Whitechapel C1870 1900
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In Anglo-Saxon England, which system made groups of ten men responsible for each other's behaviour?
questions.explain: In the tithing, men over twelve were grouped to keep one another in order and report crimes.

questions.q: In early-modern England, the crime of heresy referred to what?
options: Holding religious beliefs against the official Church
Refusing to pay the Poll Tax
questions.explain: Heresy meant holding beliefs that contradicted the established Church, and could be punished by burning.

questions.q: Two rival police forces investigated the Whitechapel murders: the Metropolitan Police and which other?
questions.explain: The City of London Police also investigated, and rivalry between forces hampered the inquiry.

questions.q: Which 1605 conspiracy is the most famous example of treason in early-modern England?
questions.explain: The 1605 Gunpowder Plot, led by Guy Fawkes, aimed to blow up Parliament and the king.

questions.q: The Norman 'murdrum' fine punished a whole community if what happened?
options: A Norman was murdered and the killer was not found
A trial by ordeal was refused
A Saxon failed to attend church
questions.explain: The murdrum fine was charged on a hundred if a Norman was found murdered and the culprit unknown.

questions.q: In Anglo-Saxon law, a 'wergild' was best described as what?
options: A trial held in a forest
A compensation payment made to a victim or their family
questions.explain: The wergild was a 'blood price' paid to the victim's family to prevent feuds.

questions.q: The Victorian 'separate system' in prisons aimed to do what?
options: House men and women in different prisons
Separate prisoners by the crime they committed
Keep prisoners in total isolation and silence to encourage reflection
questions.explain: The separate system isolated prisoners in individual cells, intending solitude to reform them.

questions.q: In Whitechapel in 1888, why did newspapers play a major role in the Ripper case?
options: They kept the murders completely secret
They spread sensational stories and increased public fear and pressure on police
They banned all reporting of crime
questions.explain: Sensational press coverage heightened public panic and put intense pressure on the police.

questions.q: Which Home Secretary set up the Metropolitan Police, giving 'Peelers' and 'Bobbies' their nickname?
questions.explain: Robert Peel's 1829 reform gave the police their popular nicknames 'Peelers' and 'Bobbies'.

questions.q: Why were so few of the Bloody Code's death sentences actually carried out in the 18th century?
options: The king personally tried every case
Juries and judges often showed leniency, reducing sentences or pardoning offenders
questions.explain: Many juries refused to convict, or judges reduced punishments, because death seemed too harsh.

questions.q: In which year was the Metropolitan Police force founded?
questions.explain: Sir Robert Peel established the Metropolitan Police in London in 1829.

questions.q: Which feature of Whitechapel made policing especially difficult in the 1880s?
options: Overcrowded slums, poor lighting and narrow alleys
A lack of any local population
questions.explain: Whitechapel's dark, crowded slums and maze of alleys hampered detection and let suspects escape.

questions.q: The Norman 'Forest Laws' chiefly made which activity a crime?
questions.explain: Forest Laws reserved hunting and timber in royal forests for the king, criminalising ordinary villagers.

questions.q: The 'Bloody Code' refers to what feature of 18th-century English justice?
options: The use of torture to extract confessions
The trial of the dead in court
The large number of crimes punishable by death
questions.explain: The Bloody Code listed over 200 crimes, even minor theft, as capital offences punishable by hanging.

questions.q: In 1823 Robert Peel's Gaols Act tried to reform prisons by introducing what?
options: Paid jailers, inspections and basic standards in prisons
questions.explain: Peel's Gaols Act of 1823 introduced inspections and paid jailers to improve prison conditions.

questions.q: During the 20th century, the abolition of the death penalty for murder in Britain took place in which decade?
questions.explain: Capital punishment for murder was suspended in 1965 and effectively abolished in the 1960s.

questions.q: The 1888 Whitechapel murders were attributed to which unidentified killer?
questions.explain: The unsolved Whitechapel murders of 1888 were blamed on the figure known as Jack the Ripper.

questions.q: From the late 18th century, transportation usually meant sending convicts to where?
questions.explain: After American independence, convicts were transported to Australia from 1787 as an alternative to hanging.

questions.q: Public executions in Britain were abolished in which year, moving hangings inside prisons?
questions.explain: From 1868, executions were carried out privately within prison walls rather than before crowds.

questions.q: In the medieval period, 'trial by ordeal' was believed to reveal guilt through whose judgement?
questions.explain: Trial by ordeal assumed God would protect the innocent, for example by healing a burn cleanly.

questions.q: Elizabeth Fry is remembered for her early 19th-century campaign to improve conditions for whom?
questions.explain: Elizabeth Fry campaigned for better, more humane treatment of women in prisons such as Newgate.

questions.q: In the medieval 'hue and cry', what were villagers expected to do?
options: Pay a fine to the lord
Chase and help catch a fleeing criminal
Report to the king in person
questions.explain: When the hue and cry was raised, all who heard it had to join the chase to catch the criminal.
